claim: Cytoplasmic dynein plays critical roles within the developing and mature nervous systems, including effecting nuclear migration and retrograde transport of various cargos.
source: Cytoplasmic dynein plays critical roles within the developing and mature nervous systems, including effecting nuclear migration, and retrograde transport of various cargos.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that summarizes established knowledge about dynein's roles in the nervous system.

claim: Mutations in dynein are causative of various developmental neuropathies and motor neuron diseases.
source: Unsurprisingly, mutations in dynein are causative of various developmental neuropathies and motor neuron diseases.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature establishing the link between dynein mutations and disease.

claim: Seventeen disease-correlated dynein mutants were characterized using budding yeast as a screening platform.
source: To circumvent complications associated with dynein studies in human cells, we employed budding yeast as a screening platform to characterize the motility properties of seventeen disease-correlated dynein mutants.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach taken in the study, which is detailed throughout the manuscript.

claim: The molecular basis for several classes of etiologically related diseases was determined using the yeast system.
source: Using this system, we determined the molecular basis for several classes of etiologically related diseases.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental results presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Compensatory mutations alleviated mutant phenotypes in two cases, one of which was confirmed with recombinant human dynein.
source: Moreover, by engineering compensatory mutations, we alleviated the mutant phenotypes in two of these cases, one of which we confirmed with recombinant human dynein.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing rescue of R1852C and H3639P mutants.

claim: The type of disease may be dictated by the degree of dynein dysfunction.
source: In addition to revealing molecular insight into dynein regulation, our data provide additional evidence that the type of disease may in fact be dictated by the degree of dynein dysfunction.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the correlation analysis between CDD scores and disease types presented in Figure 8.

claim: Neurofilaments are transported to the axon terminus by kinesins.
source: For example, neurofilaments, which provide structural stability to a cell, are transported to the axon terminus by plus end-directed microtubule motors (kinesins; Xia et al., 2003)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Xia et al., 2003.

claim: Neurofilaments are transported to the soma by cytoplasmic dynein.
source: neurofilaments, which provide structural stability to a cell, are transported to the axon terminus by plus end-directed microtubule motors (kinesins; Xia et al., 2003) and to the soma by the minus end-directed microtubule motor, cytoplasmic dynein (hereafter referred to as dynein) (He et al., 2005; Wagner et al., 2004; Shah et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to He et al., 2005; Wagner et al., 2004; Shah et al., 2000.

claim: Dynein plays a key role in trafficking numerous neuronal cargoes including autophagosomes, mitochondria, and ionotropic glutamate receptors.
source: Dynein has also been shown to play a key role in trafficking numerous other neuronal cargoes in various model organisms (He et al., 2005; Wagner et al., 2004; Shah et al., 2000; Bowman et al., 2000; Berg et al., 2000; Barkus et al., 2008; Hendricks et al., 2010; Rosa-Ferreira and Munro, 2011; Maday et al., 2012; Kamal et al., 2000; Lazarov et al., 2005; Fu and Holzbaur, 2013; Almenar-Queralt et al., 2014; Rao et al., 2017), including autophagosomes (Ravikumar et al., 2005; Katsumata et al., 2010; Cheng et al., 2015), mitochondria, and ionotropic glutamate receptors (Horak et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Defects in dynein function lead to mislocalization of cargoes and accumulation of protein aggregates at the neurite tip.
source: Defects or perturbations in dynein function lead to mislocalization of these cargoes, and results in an accumulation of protein aggregates at the neurite tip (Ravikumar et al., 2005; Levy et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Ravikumar et al., 2005; Levy et al., 2006.

claim: Accumulation of misfolded protein aggregates in the neuronal cytoplasm is a common pathological hallmark for motor neuron disease.
source: In fact, accumulation of misfolded protein aggregates in the neuronal cytoplasm is a common pathological hallmark for motor neuron disease (He et al., 2005; LaMonte et al., 2002; Lin and Schlaepfer, 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to He et al., 2005; LaMonte et al., 2002; Lin and Schlaepfer, 2006.

claim: Mouse models with dynein mutations exhibit severe neuropathy and decreased rates of retrograde axonal transport.
source: Consistent with an important role for dynein in neuronal health (Schiavo et al., 2013), mouse models with dynein mutations exhibit severe neuropathy, and decreased rates of retrograde axonal transport, among other defects (Hafezparast et al., 2003; Chen et al., 2007; Ori-McKenney et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Hafezparast et al., 2003; Chen et al., 2007; Ori-McKenney et al., 2010.

claim: Dynein promotes interkinetic nuclear migration in neuronal progenitor cells during neuronal development.
source: In addition to its key role in the retrograde trafficking of cargoes, dynein also plays a critical and conserved role during neuronal development by promoting interkinetic nuclear migration (INM) in neuronal progenitor cells, and in the subsequent migration of young postmitotic neurons. During the former process, which is critical for neurogenesis, nuclear envelope anchored dynein motors promote migration of the nucleus from the basal to the apical surface of the neuroepithelium where mitotic divisions occur (Tsai et al., 2010; Hu et al., 2013; Del Bene et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Tsai et al., 2010; Hu et al., 2013; Del Bene et al., 2008.

claim: Defects in dynein-mediated nuclear migration can lead to defects in early brain development.
source: Thus, defects in dynein-mediated nuclear migration can lead to defects in early brain development.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the established role of dynein in INM.

claim: Mutations in the dynein heavy chain (DYNC1H1 gene) are found in individuals suffering from malformations of cortical development, spinal muscular atrophy with lower extremity dominance, congenital muscular dystrophy, and Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease.
source: For instance, mutations in dynein underlie many cases of malformations of cortical development (MCD), spinal muscular atrophy with lower extremity dominance (SMA-LED), congenital muscular dystrophy (CMD), and Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (CMT) (Harms et al., 2012; Tsurusaki et al., 2012; Scoto et al., 2015; Peeters et al., 2015; Strickland et al., 2015; Weedon et al., 2011; Fiorillo et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Mutations in the dynein regulator LIS1 are causative of lissencephaly.
source: Although mutations in the dynein regulator LIS1 are causative of the MCD disease lissencephaly (Wynshaw-Boris, 2007; Wynshaw-Boris and Gambello, 2001; Reiner et al., 1993) (characterized by a smooth brain due to reduced or absent cortical folding)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Wynshaw-Boris, 2007; Wynshaw-Boris and Gambello, 2001; Reiner et al., 1993.

claim: Mutations in dynein more often lead to polymicrogyria than lissencephaly.
source: mutations in dynein more often lead to polymicrogyria, which is characterized by excessive small folds in the cerebral cortex (Poirier et al., 2013; Laquerriere et al., 2017; Willemsen et al., 2012; Vissers et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Poirier et al., 2013; Laquerriere et al., 2017; Willemsen et al., 2012; Vissers et al., 2010.

claim: The only known function for dynein in budding yeast is to position the mitotic spindle at the future site of cytokinesis.
source: In contrast to animal cells in which dynein performs numerous functions, the only known function for dynein in budding yeast is to position the mitotic spindle at the future site of cytokinesis (Li et al., 1993; Eshel et al., 1993; Carminati and Stearns, 1997)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Li et al., 1993; Eshel et al., 1993; Carminati and Stearns, 1997.

claim: The yeast dynein complex is comprised of light, light-intermediate, intermediate, and heavy chains.
source: As in higher eukaryotes, the yeast dynein complex is comprised of light (Dyn2), light-intermediate (Dyn3), intermediate (Pac11), and heavy chains (Dyn1), the latter of which is the ATPase that powers motility along microtubules (see Figure 1A) (Markus and Lee, 2011a).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Markus and Lee, 2011a and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Each of the accessory chains in budding yeast is encoded by only a single gene.
source: Whereas in humans, the non-catalytic subunits exist in different isoforms encoded by multiple genes and tissue-specific isoforms (Pfister et al., 2006; Raaijmakers et al., 2013), each of the accessory chains in budding yeast is encoded by only a single gene, enabling simple genetic analysis and manipulation.
evidence: This statement contrasts human and yeast dynein, supported by citations to Pfister et al., 2006; Raaijmakers et al., 2013.

claim: Studies have revealed a high degree of structural similarity between yeast and human dynein.
source: Moreover, studies have revealed a high degree of structural similarity between yeast and human dynein (Carter, 2013; Schmidt and Carter, 2016), rendering structure-function studies in this organism relevant and translatable to animal cells.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Carter, 2013; Schmidt and Carter, 2016.

claim: Eight mutants exhibited varying degrees of spindle positioning defects that significantly differed from wild-type.
source: This analysis revealed that eight mutants exhibited varying degrees of spindle positioning defects that significantly differed from wild-type (Figure 1B, right).
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Figure 1B.

claim: All mutants with spindle positioning defects had substitutions in the motor domain.
source: All of those mutants with defects were those with substitutions in the motor domain, which encompasses the six AAA (ATPase associated with various cellular activities) domains, the linker element that performs the powerstroke, and the microtubule-binding domain (MTBD).
evidence: This is an observation from the spindle positioning assay results.

claim: Seven out of nine mutations linked to malformations in cortical development were among those with defects in the spindle positioning assay.
source: Seven out of the nine mutations linked to malformations in cortical development (MCD) were among those with defects in this assay, whereas none of the mutations associated with the other neurological diseases exhibited significant defects.
evidence: This is an observation from the spindle positioning assay results.

claim: H3639P exhibited spindle positioning defects as severe as loss of DYN1.
source: Although most of these mutants differed to a small but significant degree from wild-type, H3639P exhibited defects as severe as loss of DYN1 (dyn1∆).
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 1B.

claim: All mutants exhibited varying degrees of alterations in their motility parameters with respect to wild-type cells in the spindle tracking assay.
source: This analysis revealed a broader more nuanced array of defects in our library of mutants (Figure 2B–F, and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and B). Strikingly, all mutants exhibited varying degrees of alterations in their motility parameters with respect to wild-type cells.
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Figure 2.

claim: H3639P cells exhibited only 10 dynein-mediated spindle displacement events from all cells observed.
source: At the most severe end of the spectrum, H3639P cells – which also had the most severe spindle positioning phenotype – exhibited only 10 dynein-mediated spindle displacement events from all cells observed (compare to a mean of 244 events for all other strains; see Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and B for scatter plots illustrating density of datasets).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the spindle tracking assay.

claim: R1852C exhibited significant defects in all motility metrics including velocity, displacement, neck transit success, and activity parameters.
source: The mutant with the second most severe spindle positioning phenotype, R1852C, exhibited significant defects in all motility metrics, including velocity, displacement (per event), neck transit success, and the two activity parameters.
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Figure 2.

claim: K1475Q mutation led to a reduction in spindle velocity, displacement, and activity metrics.
source: Another noteworthy mutant was K1475Q, a substitution within the linker domain, the mechanical element that is responsible for the powerstroke (Figure 2—figure supplement 3). This mutation led to a reduction in spindle velocity, displacement, and also reduced the activity metrics of the motor.
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Figure 2.

claim: L2557M mutation led to a reduction in neck transit success rate.
source: Interestingly, the most striking defect we observed with L2557M was a reduction in the neck transit success rate (Figure 2D), which is the likely cause of the spindle positioning defect.
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Figure 2D.

claim: All three microtubule-binding domain mutants exhibited reductions in velocity, displacement, and neck transit success.
source: All three microtubule-binding domain (MTBD) mutants exhibited fairly similar degrees and types of defects in effecting spindle movements (reductions in velocity, displacement, and neck transit success).
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Figure 2.

claim: All three MTBD mutations mapped to the surface that makes contacts with the microtubule.
source: Structural analysis revealed that all three mutations mapped to the surface of the MTBD that makes contacts with the microtubule (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: All tail domain mutations led to altered spindle motility parameters despite none causing significant spindle positioning defects.
source: Although none of them led to significant spindle positioning defects, all of the tail domain mutations led to altered spindle motility parameters.
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Most tail domain mutations (7 out of 8) clustered to two distinct regions: adjacent to the N-terminal dimerization domain or at a surface that interfaces with the intermediate chain of a neighboring heavy chain.
source: Structural analysis revealed that most of these mutations (7 out of the 8) clustered to two distinct regions: (1) adjacent to, or within the N-terminal dimerization domain, or (2) at a surface that interfaces with the intermediate chain of a neighboring heavy chain in a two dynein:1 dynactin complex (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Dynein very rarely, if ever, forms heterodimers.
source: Although we observed a small number of motile green molecules (0.9% of the total; likely due to contaminating Dyn1-GFP molecules in the protein preparation), and a single dual labeled molecule (0.3% of the total; Figure 3B, arrow), the vast majority of motile molecules (98.8%) were exclusively red, indicating that dynein very rarely, if ever, forms heterodimers (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by the single molecule imaging data presented in Figure 3.

claim: The findings suggest a co-translational dimerization model for dynein complex assembly.
source: These findings are consistent with the notion that a small fraction of the motors are capable of overcoming folding defects to adopt a native, motility-competent conformation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the homodimerization data.

claim: All three heterozygous mutants (E545V, R1852C, H3639P) exhibited partial loss-of-function phenotypes with respect to hemizygous cells.
source: Analysis of the heterozygous mutants revealed that all three exhibited partial loss-of-function phenotypes in almost all assays with respect to the hemizygous cells, indicating that they are all indeed dominant alleles.
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Figure 3.

claim: Homodimers of mutant dynein are sufficient to compromise the activity of wild-type homodimers within the cell.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that homodimers of mutant dynein are sufficient to compromise the activity of wild-type homodimers within the cell.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the heterozygous diploid experiments.

claim: Thirteen mutants that exhibited defects in the spindle tracking assay showed some degree of motility alteration in the in vitro single molecule assay.
source: Single molecule motility analysis of each mutant revealed that thirteen of those that exhibited defects in the spindle tracking assay showed some degree of motility alteration in the in vitro assay (Figure 4; see Figure 4—figure supplement 1 for scatter plots and some example kymographs).
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Figure 4.

claim: R241L, N283R, and K1475Q all led to an increase in velocity in single molecule assays.
source: Although most mutants exhibited loss-of-function phenotypes in the in vitro assay, a few mutations led to gain-of-functions. For instance, R241L, N283R, and K1475Q all led to an increase in velocity
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Figure 4.

claim: K1475Q caused an increase in run length and a small but significant increase in the fraction of active motors.
source: while K1475Q also caused an increase in run length and a small but significant increase in the fraction of active motors (see Figure 4—figure supplement 1C for example kymograph).
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Figure 4.

claim: K1475Q substitution led to a large increase in the frequency of observing cortical foci but a concomitant reduction in the number of molecules per cortical focus.
source: For instance, the K1475Q substitution (within the linker) led to a large increase in the frequency of observing cortical foci (2.2-fold; p=0.0011), but a concomitant reduction in the number of molecules per cortical focus (38% reduction in fluorescence intensity; p=0.0117)
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Figure 5.

claim: K1475Q interacts more readily with dynactin than wild-type dynein.
source: Interestingly, this analysis indeed revealed a significantly increased ratio of dynactin to dynein at plus ends (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B; from a mean of 1.07 to 1.52; p<0.0001), indicating that K1475Q interacts more readily with dynactin than wild-type dynein
evidence: This is supported by the ratiometric imaging data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: K1475Q mutation may be disrupting a potential autoinhibited state of yeast dynein.
source: and that this mutation may in fact be disrupting a potential autoinhibited state of yeast dynein.
evidence: This is an inference based on the increased dynactin binding and comparison to human dynein studies.

claim: Gain of proline is the reason for dynein dysfunction in H3639P.
source: None of these substitutions led to significant spindle positioning defects, indicating that gain of proline is the reason for dynein dysfunction in H3639P (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by the data from substitution experiments presented in Figure 6B.

claim: Introduction of a proline at two distinct sites within the inter-helical loop (positions 3639 and 3641) are sufficient to severely compromise dynein function.
source: We next asked if proline substitutions are tolerated at other sites within this inter-helical loop. Using the spindle positioning assay, we found that proline was well tolerated at all sites within the inter-helical loop except for position 3641 (2 residues C-terminal to 3639; Figure 6B). Thus, introduction of a proline at two distinct sites within this loop are sufficient to severely compromise dynein function.
evidence: This is supported by the data from proline scanning experiments presented in Figure 6B.

claim: The triple mutant F3638G H3639P W3640G exhibited spindle positioning defects that were significantly less severe than H3639P.
source: Strikingly, however, the triple mutant – in which P3639 is flanked by glycines (i.e., F3638G H3639P W3640G) – exhibited spindle positioning defects that were significantly less severe than H3639P (p<0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Figure 6B.

claim: The activity of the triple mutant F3638G H3639P W3640G was significantly greater than the H3639P single mutant in the spindle tracking assay.
source: Although the activity of this mutant was much less than that of wild-type dynein-expressing cells, it was significantly greater than the H3639P single mutant (p≤0.0361; Figure 6C–E).
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Figure 6C-E.

claim: The triple mutant does not rescue dynein motility but some other metric of in vivo dynein activity.
source: Interestingly, the single molecule assay revealed that the triple mutant was no better than the single mutant in any metrics (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E–I). This indicates that the triple mutant does not rescue dynein motility, but some other metric of in vivo dynein (or dynein-dynactin) activity.
evidence: This is supported by comparing in vivo and in vitro data in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: MG132 treatment increased the frequency of plus end targeting of H3639P by 3.7-fold to levels comparable to wild-type dynein.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, MG132 treatment increased the frequency of plus end targeting of H3639P by 3.7-fold (p<0.0001) to levels comparable to wild-type dynein
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Figure 6G.

claim: An ectopic disulfide bond is the likely cause for R1852C dysfunction.
source: Taken together, these findings indicate that an ectopic disulfide bond is the likely cause for R1852C dysfunction.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the rescue experiments with C1822S mutation.

claim: C1822S was sufficient to significantly rescue the single molecule velocity defect in the minimal dynein fragment GST-dynein331.
source: Consistent with the spindle tracking data, C1822S was indeed sufficient to significantly rescue the single molecule velocity defect in the minimal dynein fragment (Figure 7E and Figure 7—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Figure 7E.

claim: Substitution of the closely apposed cysteine to a serine (C1932S) was sufficient to restore some of the lost function in human dynein R1962C mutant.
source: Consistent with previous findings, the single R1962C mutation (equivalent to R1852C) was sufficient to completely disrupt microtubule gliding activity (Hoang et al., 2017) (Figure 7F–H); however, as with yeast dynein, substitution of the closely apposed cysteine to a serine (C1932S) was sufficient to restore some of the lost function.
evidence: This is supported by the microtubule gliding assay data presented in Figure 7F-H.

claim: On average, mutations within the highly conserved motor domain exhibited more statistically significant differences from wild-type than those in the tail domain.
source: Unsurprisingly, on average, mutations within the highly conserved motor domain exhibited more statistically significant differences from wild-type than those in the tail domain.
evidence: This is an observation from the heat map analysis in Figure 8A.

claim: More severe loss-of-function mutants appeared to correlate with MCD, while those with lesser defects mainly correlate with motor neuron diseases.
source: Moreover, this broad view of dysfunction in the mutant library revealed that the more severe loss-of-function mutants appeared to correlate with MCD, while those with lesser defects mainly correlate with motor neuron diseases (SMA-LED, CMT or CMD).
evidence: This is an observation from the heat map and CDD analysis in Figure 8.

claim: Above a CDD value of approximately 18, the likelihood of the mutation correlating with MCD increased, while its correlation with SMA-LED, CMT or CMD decreased.
source: Specifically, we found that above a CDD value of ~ 18, the likelihood of the mutation correlating with MCD increased, while its correlation with SMA-LED, CMT or CMD decreased.
evidence: This is supported by the CDD analysis presented in Figure 8B.

claim: There exists a lower threshold of dynein activity that is required for neurological development.
source: This suggests that the two general types of diseases (motor neuron disease, and defects in brain development) are each caused by different degrees of dynein dysfunction, and that there exists a lower threshold of dynein activity that is required for neurological development (see Discussion).
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between CDD scores and disease types.

claim: Motor neuron diseases appear to be more susceptible to even small degrees of dysfunction (CDD from 5 to 18).
source: Specifically, motor neuron diseases appear to be more susceptible to even small degrees of dysfunction (CDD from 5 to 18), while MCD tends to correlate with larger degrees of dynein dysfunction (CDD ≥ 19).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the CDD analysis and disease correlation.

claim: MCD tends to correlate with larger degrees of dynein dysfunction (CDD ≥ 19).
source: Specifically, motor neuron diseases appear to be more susceptible to even small degrees of dysfunction (CDD from 5 to 18), while MCD tends to correlate with larger degrees of dynein dysfunction (CDD ≥ 19).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the CDD analysis and disease correlation.

claim: The differences in disease susceptibility are due to the distinct types of dynein-mediated transport required to maintain motor neuron health versus that required to effect nuclear or neuronal migration in the developing neocortex.
source: The reasons for this are unclear, but we hypothesize that the differences are due to the somewhat distinct types of dynein-mediated transport required to maintain motor neuron health, versus that required to effect nuclear or neuronal migration in the developing neocortex.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed in the Discussion to explain the disease correlation findings.

claim: Motor neurons possess extremely long axons (≤1 m) and require a high degree of processive transport for vesicular cargoes.
source: Motor neurons possess extremely long axons (≤1 m), and thus require a high degree of processive transport for the myriad vesicular cargoes that are moved from the soma to the axon terminal and back.
evidence: This is established knowledge about motor neuron biology.

claim: Even subtle loss-of-functions in dynein-mediated transport can, over time, compromise motor neuron health.
source: Thus, it stands to reason that even subtle loss-of-functions in dynein-mediated transport can, over time, compromise motor neuron health.
evidence: This is an inference based on the requirements of motor neurons and the disease correlation data.

claim: During INM and neuronal migration, many dynein molecules are likely engaging with microtubules to effect neurogenesis.
source: Thus, for both INM and neuronal migration, many dynein molecules are likely engaging with microtubules to effect neurogenesis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the biology of INM and neuronal migration.

claim: The minimal functional requirements for individual dynein motors during INM or neuronal migration are potentially lower due to the large number of motors engaged during a migration event.
source: Thus, the minimal functional requirements for individual dynein motors during INM or neuronal migration are potentially lower due to the large number of motors engaged during a migration event.
evidence: This is an inference to explain the differential disease susceptibility.

claim: Teams of motors comprised of a mixture of wild-type and mutant variants can work together to effect INM, but are less able to effectively transport single vesicular cargoes along the axon.
source: In such a scenario, teams of motors comprised of a mixture of wild-type and mutant variants (due to the heterozygous nature of these diseases) can work together to effect INM, but are less able to effectively transport single vesicular cargoes along the axon.
evidence: This is a hypothesis to explain the differential disease susceptibility based on motor requirements.
